orig_coordinate_geometry_distance_midpoi.description: Learn distance and midpoint methods for Cambridge 9709 Pure 1. Find exact lengths, missing endpoints, equally distant points and a circle from its diameter.

sections.title: How do coordinate changes give a length?
sections.label: Find the distance
sections.intro: From \(A(-3,1)\) to \(B(5,5)\), move \(8\) units right and \(4\) units up. These are the two perpendicular sides of a right-angled triangle. The segment \(AB\) is its hypotenuse.

blocks.html:
Subtract the \(x\)-coordinates to get \(\Delta x=x_2-x_1\). Do the same for \(y\). Then use Pythagoras.

\[AB=\sqrt{(\Delta x)^2+(\Delta y)^2}.\]
Write \((-8)^2=64\). Squaring a signed coordinate change is different from placing a minus sign in front of a square.

blocks.prompt: Find the length of the segment from \(P(-4,2)\) to \(Q(2,-6)\).
blocks.hint: The coordinate changes are \(6\) and \(-8\). Square each before adding.

retry.feedback: \(100\) is the squared length. Take its square root to get \(PQ\).
Adding the horizontal and vertical distances gives the length of a two-leg route. Use Pythagoras for the straight segment.

blocks.prompt: Find the exact length from \(P(-2,4)\) to \(Q(1,-4)\). Give a surd.
blocks.hint: Use \(\Delta x=3\) and \(\Delta y=-8\). Keep the final square root exact.

retry.feedback: You found \(PQ^2\). Give \(\sqrt{73}\) for the length.
Use \(3^2+(-8)^2\) under the square root. The negative \(y\)-change contributes \(64\).

sections.title: Where is the midpoint?
sections.label: Find the midpoint
sections.intro: To reach the midpoint of \(AB\), make half of each move from \(A\) to \(B\). From \((-3,1)\), move \(4\) right and \(2\) up to reach \(C(1,3)\).

blocks.html:
Average the two \(x\)-coordinates and average the two \(y\)-coordinates. Keep the coordinates in that order.

\[C=\left(\frac{x_1+x_2}{2},\,\frac{y_1+y_2}{2}\right).\]
Check each midpoint coordinate lies between the two endpoint coordinates. When one coordinate is the same at both ends, it stays the same at the midpoint.

blocks.prompt: Find the midpoint of \(P(-6,1)\) and \(Q(4,6)\).
blocks.hint: The \(x\)-coordinate is halfway from \(-6\) to \(4\). The \(y\)-coordinate is halfway from \(1\) to \(6\).

retry.feedback: Divide each coordinate sum by \(2\) to find its average.
These are half the coordinate changes from \(P\). Add them to \(P\) to get the midpoint.

sections.title: How can a midpoint locate the missing endpoint?
sections.label: Recover an endpoint
sections.intro: The move from \(A\) to the midpoint \(C\) is exactly the move from \(C\) to \(B\). Knowing \(A\) and \(C\) therefore tells you the position of \(B\).

blocks.html: Write \(B_x=2C_x-A_x\) and \(B_y=2C_y-A_y\). These are the midpoint equations rearranged for the missing coordinates.
The change from a point to the midpoint is a displacement. Add it to the midpoint to turn that move into the final position.

blocks.prompt: A segment starts at \((3,-2)\) and has midpoint \((-1,\tfrac52)\). Find the other endpoint.
blocks.hint: Double each midpoint coordinate and subtract the matching coordinate of the known endpoint.

retry.feedback: That is the move to the midpoint. Repeat that move starting from the midpoint to locate the far endpoint.
Each doubled midpoint coordinate is the sum of two endpoint coordinates. Subtract the known endpoint.

sections.title: How can equal distances locate a point?
sections.label: Use equal distances
sections.intro: A point \(P\) lies on the \(y\)-axis and is equally far from \(A\) and \(B\). Write it as \(P(0,p)\). Now there is only one unknown coordinate.

blocks.html: Distances are non-negative, so \(PA=PB\) is equivalent to \(PA^2=PB^2\). Equate the sums of squares. The squared terms in the unknown coordinate cancel.
Use the given restriction before expanding. If the point lies on the \(x\)-axis, its \(y\)-coordinate is zero.

blocks.prompt: Find the point on the \(x\)-axis equally far from \(D(-2,3)\) and \(E(4,1)\).
blocks.solution: Equating squared distances gives \(4x+13=-8x+17\), so \(12x=4\). The point is \((\tfrac13,0)\).

retry.feedback: That is the midpoint of \(DE\). It is equidistant, but the required point must have \(y=0\).
The number \(\tfrac13\) is the \(x\)-coordinate. A point on the \(x\)-axis has \(y=0\).

sections.title: How does a diameter determine a circle?
sections.label: Use a diameter
sections.intro: When \(AB\) is a diameter, the centre is its midpoint \(C\). The radius runs from \(C\) to one endpoint.

blocks.html: Find the midpoint for the centre. Since \(r=AB/2\), the squared radius is \(r^2=AB^2/4\). You can also find \(r^2\) by using the squared distance from the centre to one endpoint.
The radius is half a length. Dividing the squared diameter by \(2\) does not give the squared radius.

blocks.prompt: A circle has diameter from \((-2,4)\) to \((6,-2)\). Give its centre.
blocks.hint: Find the midpoint of the two ends of the diameter.

retry.feedback: These are the half-diameter coordinate changes. Add them to \((-2,4)\) to find the centre.

blocks.prompt: For the same diameter from \((-2,4)\) to \((6,-2)\), find \(r^2\).
blocks.hint: The diameter's squared length is \(8^2+(-6)^2=100\). Square the factor \(\tfrac12\) when finding \(r^2\).
blocks.solution: The radius is half of \(10\), so \(r=5\) and \(r^2=25\).

retry.feedback: Halving the length quarters its square. Use \(100/4\).
\(5\) is the radius. The question asks for its square.
That is the squared diameter. First halve the diameter, or divide its square by \(4\).

examples.title: Use the two sides of the right triangle
examples.question: Find the exact distance between \(A(-3,1)\) and \(B(5,5)\).
solution: The coordinate changes from \(A\) to \(B\) are \(5-(-3)=8\) and \(5-1=4\).
Squaring and adding gives \(AB^2=8^2+4^2=64+16=80\).
Take the non-negative square root. \(AB=\sqrt{80}=4\sqrt5\).

examples.title: Average one coordinate at a time
examples.question: Use the midpoint formula for \(A(-3,1)\) and \(B(5,5)\).
solution: The average \(x\)-coordinate is \(\frac{-3+5}{2}=1\).
The average \(y\)-coordinate is \(\frac{1+5}{2}=3\). So \(C=(1,3)\).
The move from \(A\) to \(C\) is \((4,2)\), and the move from \(C\) to \(B\) is also \((4,2)\).

examples.title: Extend the same half of a segment
examples.question: The midpoint of \(AB\) is \(C(1,3)\) and \(A=(-3,1)\). Find \(B\).
solution: From \(A\) to \(C\), the change is \(1-(-3)=4\) in \(x\) and \(3-1=2\) in \(y\).
Add the same changes to \(C\). This gives \(B=(1+4,3+2)=(5,5)\).
Check that the averages of the endpoint coordinates are \(1\) and \(3\).

examples.title: Find an equidistant point on the y-axis
examples.question: Find the point \(P(0,p)\) that is equally far from \(A(-3,1)\) and \(B(5,5)\).
solution: At \(P=(0,5)\), the two squared distances are \(9+16=25\) and \(25+0=25\).

examples.title: Use the midpoint and half the diameter
examples.question: A circle has diameter from \(A(-3,1)\) to \(B(5,5)\). Find its centre and the square of its radius.
solution: The midpoint is \((1,3)\), so this is the centre.
The diameter has squared length \(80\), so \(r^2=80/4=20\).
Check using the changes from the centre to \(B\). They are \(4\) and \(2\). Thus \(4^2+2^2=20\), and \(r=2\sqrt5\).

glossary.definition: The signed changes in \(x\) and \(y\) between two points.
The point halfway along a segment.
At the same distance from each named point.
A chord passing through the centre of a circle. Its length is twice the radius.

revision.body:
Difference for distance, average for midpoint

For \(A(x_1,y_1)\) and \(B(x_2,y_2)\), use \(AB=\sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2}\). The midpoint averages the two \(x\)-coordinates and the two \(y\)-coordinates separately.

Work backwards from the midpoint

If \(C\) is the midpoint, \(B_x=2C_x-A_x\) and \(B_y=2C_y-A_y\). Repeat the same move from \(A\) to \(C\), starting at \(C\).

Turn a condition into an equation

For equal distances, use \(PA^2=PB^2\). If \(AB\) is a diameter, the centre is its midpoint and \(r^2=AB^2/4\).
revision.checks:
• Subtract coordinates in the same order.
  • Keep a length exact until taking the final root.
  • Check both coordinates of the midpoint or missing end.
revision.examTip: Write a point on the \(x\)-axis as \((x,0)\) before imposing an equal-distance condition. Read whether the question asks for \(r\) or \(r^2\).

orig_coordinate_geometry_parallel_perpen.description: Learn gradients, parallel and perpendicular lines, and perpendicular bisectors for Cambridge 9709 Pure 1. Handle horizontal and vertical lines and solve for an unknown coordinate.

sections.title: How do I find the gradient with the correct sign?
sections.label: Find the gradient
sections.intro: The segment from \(A(-3,1)\) to \(B(5,5)\) rises \(4\) units in a horizontal run of \(8\). The gradient measures the signed rise per unit of run.

blocks.html: Use \(m=\frac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1}\), with \(x_2\ne x_1\). A line falling as you move right has negative gradient. A vertical line has undefined gradient because the horizontal change is zero.
If you take the second point minus the first in the numerator, use the same order in the denominator.

blocks.prompt: Find the gradient of the line through \((-2,4)\) and \((4,0)\).
blocks.hint: When moving left to right, the run is \(6\) and the \(y\)-coordinate falls by \(4\).

retry.feedback: The line falls as you move right. Keep the negative sign in the change in \(y\).
You divided the run by the rise. Gradient is signed rise divided by run.

sections.title: What stays the same on a parallel line?
sections.label: Find a parallel
sections.intro: A parallel line follows the same direction as the original line. Its position is fixed by the point it must pass through.

blocks.html: For non-vertical lines, use the same gradient and substitute the required point. For \(ax+by+c=0\), first rearrange to \(y=-\frac ab x-\frac cb\) if \(b\ne0\). Distinct vertical lines are parallel.
Matching gradients give the same direction. If the two lines also contain the same point, their equations describe one line.

blocks.prompt: Find the equation of the line through \((6,1)\) parallel to \(3x+2y=8\).
blocks.hint: Keep \(3x+2y\) on the left and find the constant by substituting \((6,1)\).
blocks.solution: Use \(3(6)+2(1)=20\), so the new line is \(3x+2y=20\). Both lines have gradient \(-\tfrac32\).

retry.feedback: The gradient is right. Recalculate the constant using the required point \((6,1)\).
Your line passes through the point, but it rises to the right. The given line has negative gradient.

sections.title: Why is the perpendicular gradient a negative reciprocal?
sections.label: Find a perpendicular
sections.intro: On \(AB\), a step of \(4\) right and \(2\) up has gradient \(\tfrac12\). Rotating that step a quarter turn anticlockwise gives \(2\) left and \(4\) up. The perpendicular gradient is \(-2\).

blocks.html: Rotating a step \((a,b)\) through \(90^\circ\) anticlockwise gives \((-b,a)\). If \(a\) and \(b\) are non-zero, the two gradients are \(b/a\) and \(-a/b\). Their product is \(-1\).
Check \(m_1m_2=-1\) only when both gradients are finite. Handle an axis-parallel line using its direction.

blocks.prompt: Find the line through \((3,2)\) perpendicular to \(y=-\tfrac23x+5\).
blocks.hint: The negative reciprocal of \(-\tfrac23\) is \(\tfrac32\). Use this gradient through \((3,2)\).

retry.feedback: Taking the reciprocal alone leaves a negative gradient. Changing the sign as well gives \(\tfrac32\).
Your line changes the sign but keeps the size of the gradient. Swap the numerator and denominator as well.

sections.title: What makes a perpendicular line a bisector?
sections.label: Bisect the segment
sections.intro: The perpendicular line in the sketch passes through \(C(1,3)\), the midpoint of \(AB\). These two conditions give one perpendicular bisector.

blocks.html: First find the midpoint, then find the perpendicular direction. Use both in the equation. Points on the perpendicular bisector are equally far from the endpoints.
Check the midpoint lies on the final line. A slope calculation alone leaves many possible perpendicular lines.

blocks.prompt: Find the perpendicular bisector of the segment from \((-1,1)\) to \((5,3)\).
blocks.hint: Find midpoint \((2,2)\) and segment gradient \(\tfrac13\). The bisector has gradient \(-3\).

retry.feedback: This perpendicular goes through the first endpoint. A bisector must pass through the midpoint \((2,2)\).
This is the line containing the segment. Use the negative reciprocal of its gradient through the midpoint.

sections.title: What if a line is horizontal or vertical?
sections.label: Axis-parallel lines
sections.intro: Horizontal lines have constant \(y\). Vertical lines have constant \(x\). They are perpendicular to each other.

blocks.html:
DirectionEquationGradient
Horizontal\(y=c\)Zero
Vertical\(x=c\)Undefined
A gradient of zero gives a horizontal line. Division by zero signals a vertical line, so use \(x=c\) directly.

blocks.prompt: Find the perpendicular bisector of the segment from \((-5,4)\) to \((1,4)\).
blocks.hint: The segment is horizontal. Find its midpoint and write the vertical line through it.
blocks.solution: The midpoint is \((-2,4)\), so the perpendicular bisector is \(x=-2\).

retry.feedback: This is the horizontal line through both endpoints. The bisector runs vertically through the midpoint.
The midpoint has \(x=-2\). A vertical line fixes that \(x\)-coordinate.

blocks.prompt: Find the line parallel to \(y=-4\) that passes through \((3,2)\).
blocks.hint: Keep the horizontal direction and use the \(y\)-coordinate of the required point.
blocks.solution: The line is \(y=2\). It has gradient zero and contains \((3,2)\).

retry.feedback: The point is on your line, but \(x=3\) is vertical. A horizontal line has fixed \(y\).

sections.title: How can a direction fix a missing coordinate?
sections.label: Find a parameter
sections.intro: When one coordinate is unknown, start from the required direction. That gives an equation for the coordinate change.

blocks.html: Find the required gradient first. If a denominator contains the unknown, note the value that would make it zero. Check the chosen coordinate in the original direction condition.
Substituting the value back into the gradient catches sign and zero-denominator errors.

blocks.prompt: The segment joining \((t,-1)\) and \((4,5)\) is parallel to \(y=2x+3\). Find \(t\).
blocks.hint: The rise is \(6\). A gradient of \(2\) requires a horizontal change of \(3\).

retry.feedback: At \(t=7\), the rise is \(6\) and the run is \(-3\), so the gradient is \(-2\). Use a run of \(3\).
At \(t=4\), the segment is vertical and has undefined gradient. The gradient here must be \(2\).

examples.title: Use the same subtraction order twice
examples.question: Find the gradient from \(A(-3,1)\) to \(B(5,5)\). Check it by reversing the order.
solution: From \(A\) to \(B\), the rise is \(4\) and the run is \(8\), so \(m=\tfrac12\).
From \(B\) to \(A\), the changes are \(-4\) and \(-8\). The ratio is still \(\frac{-4}{-8}=\tfrac12\).

examples.title: Keep the gradient and move the line
examples.question: Find the line parallel to \(AB\) that passes through \((1,-2)\). The gradient of \(AB\) is \(\tfrac12\).
solution: Using \(y-y_1=m(x-x_1)\) through the given point gives \(y+2=\tfrac12(x-1)\).
Multiply by \(2\) and rearrange to \(x-2y=5\). The original line and this line have the same gradient.
Check \(1-2(-2)=5\), so the new line contains \((1,-2)\).

examples.title: Use the perpendicular direction through a new point
examples.question: Find the line through \((2,4)\) perpendicular to \(AB\), whose gradient is \(\tfrac12\).
solution: The perpendicular gradient is \(-1/(\tfrac12)=-2\).
Using the given point gives \(y-4=-2(x-2)\). This becomes \(2x+y=8\).
The product of the gradients is \(-1\), and the point gives \(2(2)+4=8\).

examples.title: Use the direction and the midpoint
examples.question: Find the perpendicular bisector of \(A(-3,1)\) and \(B(5,5)\).
solution: The midpoint is \((1,3)\) and the segment gradient is \(4/8=\tfrac12\).
The bisector has gradient \(-2\) and passes through \((1,3)\). Its equation is \(y-3=-2(x-1)\), or \(2x+y=5\).
The line meets the \(y\)-axis at \((0,5)\), the point found earlier by equating the distances to \(A\) and \(B\).

examples.title: Bisect a vertical segment
examples.question: Find the perpendicular bisector of \((-2,-1)\) and \((-2,7)\).
solution: The segment is vertical because its endpoints have the same \(x\)-coordinate.
The midpoint is \((-2,3)\). A perpendicular is horizontal, so its equation is \(y=3\).

examples.title: Use a perpendicular gradient to locate an endpoint
examples.question: The segment from \((t,1)\) to \((3,5)\) is perpendicular to \(y=-2x+1\). Find \(t\).
solution: The required gradient is \(\tfrac12\). In particular the segment has non-zero horizontal change.
The changes are \(8\) horizontally and \(4\) vertically. Their ratio gives \(\tfrac12\).

glossary.definition: Signed change in \(y\) per unit change in \(x\) along a non-vertical line.
Meeting at a right angle.
The line through the midpoint of a segment at right angles to it.
Equations that describe the same line.

revision.body:
Read and compare gradients

Use \(m=(y_2-y_1)/(x_2-x_1)\) when \(x_2\ne x_1\). Compare like orders of subtraction.

Given lineParallel directionPerpendicular direction
Finite, non-zero \(m\)Same \(m\)\(-1/m\)
HorizontalHorizontal, \(y=c\)Vertical, \(x=c\)
VerticalVertical, \(x=c\)Horizontal, \(y=c\)

Make a perpendicular bisector

Find the segment midpoint and the perpendicular direction. Write the line through that midpoint. In the sketch, \(AB\) has gradient \(\tfrac12\) and midpoint \((1,3)\). The bisector is \(y-3=-2(x-1)\).
revision.checks:
• Check both direction and required point.
  • Use the negative reciprocal for a finite, non-zero gradient.
  • Use a constant coordinate for a vertical or horizontal line.
revision.examTip: For a bisector, show the midpoint calculation as well as the direction. Two lines of equal finite gradient through the same point coincide.

orig_coordinate_geometry_straight_lines.description: Work with straight-line equations for Cambridge 9709 Pure 1. Use a point and gradient, find exact intercepts and intersections, and calculate the area bounded by a line and the axes.

sections.title: Which form uses the given point and gradient?
sections.label: Point and gradient
sections.intro: The line \(AB\) has gradient \(\tfrac12\) and passes through \(A(-3,1)\). Writing the changes from \(A\) gives the equation in one step.

blocks.html: For a point \((x_1,y_1)\) and finite gradient \(m\), write \(y-y_1=m(x-x_1)\). In \(y=mx+c\), \(c\) is the \(y\)-intercept. The general form \(ax+by+c=0\) can also describe a vertical line when \(b=0\) and \(a\ne0\).
Substitute the given point into your finished equation. When clearing fractions, multiply the whole equation by the same non-zero number.

blocks.prompt: Find the line through \((4,-2)\) with gradient \(-\tfrac34\).
blocks.hint: Use \(y-(-2)=-\tfrac34(x-4)\). Multiply every term by \(4\) to clear the fraction.

retry.feedback: The gradient is correct. The point has \(y=-2\), so the constant is \(3(4)+4(-2)=4\).
The line through the point must fall to the right. Keep the gradient \(-\tfrac34\).

sections.title: How do two points determine the equation?
sections.label: Use two points
sections.intro: Distinct points specify both a direction and a position. If the \(x\)-coordinates agree, the line is vertical and its equation already follows.

blocks.html: When the \(x\)-coordinates differ, find the gradient and substitute either point into \(y-y_1=m(x-x_1)\). Check the second point in the result.
If the horizontal change is zero, write \(x=x_1\) directly. A point–gradient calculation needs a finite gradient.

blocks.prompt: Find the line through \((-1,4)\) and \((5,1)\).
blocks.hint: The gradient is \(-3/6\). Then use either given point.

retry.feedback: The gradient is correct. At the first point the constant is \(-1+2(4)=7\).
Your line has positive gradient. Going from \((-1,4)\) to \((5,1)\), \(y\) decreases by \(3\).

blocks.prompt: Find the line through \((-3,1)\) and \((-3,7)\).
blocks.hint: Identify the coordinate that is the same at both points.
blocks.solution: Both points have \(x=-3\), so that is the equation of the vertical line.

retry.feedback: The matching coordinate is \(x\). The constant \(x\)-coordinate gives the vertical line \(x=-3\).

sections.title: Where does the line meet each axis?
sections.label: Find the intercepts
sections.intro: Every point on the \(x\)-axis has \(y=0\). Every point on the \(y\)-axis has \(x=0\). Use these conditions one at a time.

blocks.html: Set \(y=0\) for the \(x\)-intercept and \(x=0\) for the \(y\)-intercept. Give coordinates in the order \((x,y)\). A line that is parallel to and distinct from an axis has no intersection with that axis.
When a line coincides with an axis, every point on that axis lies on the line. Check this before looking for a single intercept.

blocks.prompt: Give the two axis intercepts of \(3x-2y=12\) as coordinate pairs.
blocks.hint: First set \(y=0\), then set \(x=0\). Preserve the negative sign in the second equation.

retry.feedback: The \(x\)-intercept is correct. With \(x=0\), solve \(-2y=12\).
You found the \(x\)-intercept. Also set \(x=0\) to find where the line meets the \(y\)-axis.
Put each answer on the axis used to find it. The \(x\)-intercept has \(y=0\) and the \(y\)-intercept has \(x=0\).

sections.title: What does a simultaneous solution represent?
sections.label: Meet at one point
sections.intro: A common point satisfies both line equations. The segment \(AB\) and its perpendicular bisector meet at their shared point \(C\).

blocks.html: Use substitution or elimination for the two equations. Recover the matching second coordinate, then check the pair in both equations. Distinct parallel lines have no common point. Coincident lines share the whole line.
A value of \(x\) is only one coordinate of the intersection. Substitute it back to obtain the paired value of \(y\).

blocks.prompt: Find the intersection of \(y=2x-1\) and \(3x+y=14\).
blocks.hint: Use \(3x+(2x-1)=14\). Find \(x\), then find the matching \(y\).
blocks.solution: \(5x=15\) gives \(x=3\). Using \(y=2x-1\) gives \(y=5\), so the point is \((3,5)\).

retry.feedback: Keep the coordinates in \((x,y)\) order. The substitution equation gives \(x=3\).
The value \(x=3\) is correct. Use \(2(3)-1\) for the second coordinate.

blocks.prompt: Give all common points of \(y=-x+4\) and \(2x+2y=10\). Enter empty if there are none.
blocks.hint: Divide the second equation by \(2\) and compare the two constants in \(x+y=c\).
blocks.solution: The equations give \(x+y=4\) and \(x+y=5\). These describe distinct parallel lines with no common points.

retry.feedback: This is on the first line. It gives \(2(0)+2(4)=8\) in the second expression, which must equal \(10\).
This is on the second line. Check it in the first equation too.

sections.title: How do the intercepts give the area?
sections.label: Area from intercepts
sections.intro: The line \(2y=x+5\) and the axes bound a right-angled triangle. The two sides from the origin have lengths \(5\) and \(\tfrac52\).

blocks.html: If the intercepts are \((p,0)\) and \((0,q)\), with both \(p\) and \(q\) non-zero, the area is \(\tfrac12|p|\,|q|\). Use the distances from the origin as lengths.
A positive intercept triangle needs two distinct non-zero intercepts. A line through the origin shares that point with both axes.

blocks.prompt: Find the area of the triangle bounded by \(4x-3y=24\) and the axes.
blocks.hint: Find each intercept and take its distance from the origin. Use half the product of those lengths.
blocks.solution: The intercepts are \((6,0)\) and \((0,-8)\). The area is \(\tfrac12(6)(8)=24\) square units.

retry.feedback: The \(y\)-intercept is negative, but the height from the origin is \(8\). Use positive lengths for the area.
You found base times height. Multiply by \(\tfrac12\) for the triangle.

examples.title: Write three forms for the same line
examples.question: Write the equation of the line through \(A(-3,1)\) with gradient \(\tfrac12\).
solution: Point and gradient give \(y-1=\tfrac12(x+3)\).
Rearrange to \(y=\tfrac12x+\tfrac52\). The constant \(\tfrac52\) is the height at \(x=0\).
Multiply by \(2\) and move all terms to one side to get \(x-2y+5=0\). The three equations describe the same line.

examples.title: Find a line through two distinct points
examples.question: Find the equation of the line through \((-2,5)\) and \((4,-1)\).
solution: The gradient is \(\frac{-1-5}{4-(-2)}=-1\).
Use the first point to get \(y-5=-(x+2)\), or \(x+y=3\).
Check the second point gives \(4+(-1)=3\).

examples.title: Find both places where AB meets an axis
examples.question: Find the two axis intercepts of \(2y=x+5\).
solution: With \(x=0\), \(2y=5\) gives \(y=\tfrac52\). The \(y\)-intercept is \((0,\tfrac52)\).

examples.title: Find the same point from two equations
examples.question: Find the intersection of \(2y=x+5\) and \(2x+y=5\).
solution: Double \(2x+y=5\) to get \(4x+2y=10\).
From \(2y=1+5\), \(y=3\). The point \((1,3)\) satisfies both equations.

examples.title: Turn signed intercepts into lengths
examples.question: Find the area of the triangle formed by \(2y=x+5\) and the axes.
solution: The intercepts are \((-5,0)\) and \((0,\tfrac52)\).
Using the base \(5\) and height \(\tfrac52\), the area is \(\tfrac12(5)(\tfrac52)=\tfrac{25}4\) square units.

glossary.definition: An equation written from a point and a finite gradient.
A point where the graph meets an axis.
A point shared by the graphs.
Equations that must be true for the same values of the variables.

revision.body:
Choose a form for the information given

You knowStart with
A point and finite gradient\(y-y_1=m(x-x_1)\)
Gradient and y-intercept\(y=mx+c\)
A fixed x-coordinate\(x=c\)

Read points from equations

Set \(y=0\) at the \(x\)-intercept and \(x=0\) at the \(y\)-intercept. The intercept triangle has area \(\tfrac12|p|\,|q|\) for non-zero intercepts \(p\) and \(q\). Solve the two equations together for an intersection.
revision.checks:
• Check the given point or points in the new line.
  • Use positive distances in an area calculation.
  • Substitute a shared point into both equations.
revision.examTip: Keep coordinates paired. Two distinct parallel lines give no common point, and coincident equations give the same line.

orig_coordinate_geometry_circles.description: Study circle equations for Cambridge 9709 Pure 1. Find the centre and radius, complete the square, use a diameter or three points, and write a tangent from its radius.

sections.title: Why does a fixed distance give a circle equation?
sections.label: Write a circle equation
sections.intro: Every point on the circle is the same distance from \(C\). The point \(B(5,5)\) is \(2\sqrt5\) units from \(C(1,3)\), so the radius is \(2\sqrt5\).

blocks.html:
For centre \((h,k)\) and positive radius \(r\), equate the squared distance from \((x,y)\) to \(r^2\).

\[(x-h)^2+(y-k)^2=r^2.\]
Read the centre by setting each bracket to zero. In \((x+2)^2\), the centre's \(x\)-coordinate is \(-2\).

blocks.prompt: Find the equation of the circle with centre \((-2,4)\) that passes through \((1,0)\).
blocks.hint: The radius has coordinate changes \(3\) and \(-4\). Calculate \(r^2\), then put the centre into the squared terms.

retry.feedback: The centre is right. The left side is a squared distance, so the right side must be \(5^2\).
The square terms must vanish at the centre \((-2,4)\). Use \(x+2\) and \(y-4\).

sections.title: How do I tell where a point lies?
sections.label: Test a point
sections.intro: Compare the point's squared distance from the centre with the squared radius. You can decide whether it lies inside, on or outside the circle using integers or exact fractions.

blocks.html: For \(d^2=(x-h)^2+(y-k)^2\), use \(d^2<r^2\) for inside, \(d^2=r^2\) for on the circle and \(d^2>r^2\) for outside.
Keep both sides in squared units throughout the comparison. Compare \(d^2\) with \(r^2\), or compare \(d\) with \(r\).

field.label: All points on the circle (x, y)

blocks.hint: Substitute each point into the left side. Only squared distances equal to \(10\) give points on the circle.
blocks.solution: The squared distances in order are \(10,10,9,16\). The points on the circle are \((2,3)\) and \((-4,1)\).

retry.feedback: This point lies on the circle. Check \((-4,1)\) as well.
This point lies on the circle. Check \((2,3)\) as well.
The first two are on the circle. The point \((-1,5)\) gives \(d^2=9\), placing it inside.

sections.title: How does expanded form reveal the centre?
sections.label: Complete two squares
sections.intro: The equation \(x^2+y^2-2x-6y-10=0\) looks different from the circle equation in the first section. Complete the square separately for \(x\) and \(y\) to reveal the same centre and radius.

blocks.html: Group the \(x\)-terms and the \(y\)-terms. Half each linear coefficient to form each square, then balance the added constants. In \(x^2+y^2+2gx+2fy+c=0\), the centre is \((-g,-f)\) and \(r^2=g^2+f^2-c\) for a real circle of positive radius.
After completing the squares, a positive right-hand side gives a circle. Zero gives just the centre point, and a negative value gives no real points.

blocks.prompt: Find the centre of \(x^2+y^2+6x-4y+4=0\).
blocks.hint: Complete \(x^2+6x\) with \(9\) and \(y^2-4y\) with \(4\). Which values make the new brackets zero?
blocks.solution: The new form is \((x+3)^2+(y-2)^2=9\). Its centre is \((-3,2)\).

retry.feedback: Set \(x+3=0\) and \(y-2=0\) to read the centre.
Halve each linear coefficient before choosing the signs of the centre coordinates.

blocks.prompt: Find the radius of \(x^2+y^2+6x-4y+4=0\).
blocks.hint: The right side after completing both squares is \(-4+9+4\). Take the square root for the radius.

retry.feedback: \(9\) is \(r^2\). Take the positive square root to get the radius.
Keep the original constant. The right side becomes \(-4+9+4=9\).

sections.title: When does a right angle identify the diameter?
sections.label: Angle in a semicircle
sections.intro: Let \(Q=(-3,5)\). The sides \(QA\) and \(QB\) are vertical and horizontal, so \(\angle AQB=90^\circ\). The side opposite that angle is \(AB\).

blocks.html: An angle subtended by a diameter at another point on the circle is a right angle. Conversely, for a right-angled triangle, the hypotenuse is the diameter of its circumcircle.
Locate the right angle first. The diameter joins the other two vertices.

blocks.prompt: Find the circle through \(U(-2,-1)\), \(V(4,3)\) and \(W(4,-1)\).
blocks.hint: The right angle is at \(W\), so the diameter is \(UV\). Use its midpoint and half its length.

retry.feedback: The midpoint is right. Halving the diameter divides its square by \(4\), giving \(52/4=13\).
\(W\) is the right-angle vertex. Use the midpoint of the opposite side \(UV\) for the centre.

sections.title: How does the radius give the tangent?
sections.label: Find a tangent
sections.intro: At \(B(5,5)\), the tangent meets radius \(CB\) at \(90^\circ\). The tangent passes through \(B\). The normal is the line along the radius.

blocks.html: Check that the given point is on the circle. Find the radius direction from centre to point. Use the perpendicular direction through the point for the tangent. A vertical radius gives a horizontal tangent, and a horizontal radius gives a vertical tangent.
The normal passes through the centre and the contact point. The tangent uses the contact point and a perpendicular direction.

blocks.prompt: A circle has centre \((-2,4)\). Its tangent touches at \((1,0)\). Find the tangent equation.
blocks.hint: The radius has gradient \(-4/3\), so the tangent has gradient \(3/4\). Use the point of contact.

retry.feedback: This is the line along the radius. Use the perpendicular gradient \(\tfrac34\).
The gradient is right. The tangent passes through \((1,0)\), the point on the circle.

blocks.prompt: A circle with centre \((2,-1)\) has contact point \((2,3)\) on a tangent. Find the tangent equation.
blocks.hint: The radius is vertical. Use a horizontal line through the contact point.
blocks.solution: The tangent fixes \(y=3\) because it is horizontal through \((2,3)\).

retry.feedback: \(x=2\) is the vertical line containing the radius. Its perpendicular through the contact point has fixed \(y\).
This line is horizontal through the centre. Use the contact point \((2,3)\).

sections.title: How can three points locate a centre?
sections.label: Find a hidden centre
sections.intro: The centre is equally far from any two points on the circumference. That puts it on the perpendicular bisector of each chord.

blocks.html: Three distinct non-collinear points determine a circle. Find the intersection of two perpendicular bisectors, or use equal squared distances to form two linear equations for the centre. Then find the radius from any one point.
Check all three points in the final equation. A circle of positive radius cannot pass through three distinct collinear points.

blocks.prompt: Find the centre of the circle through \((0,0)\), \((6,0)\) and \((2,4)\).
blocks.hint: The first chord gives a bisector \(x=3\). For centre \((3,k)\), equate squared distances to \((0,0)\) and \((2,4)\).

retry.feedback: This is the first chord's midpoint. Move along its bisector until the distance to \((2,4)\) also agrees.
\(x=3\) is correct. Use the equal squared distances \(9+k^2\) and \(1+(k-4)^2\) to determine \(k\).

blocks.prompt: Give the circle equation through the same three points \((0,0)\), \((6,0)\) and \((2,4)\).
blocks.hint: Use centre \((3,1)\) and calculate the squared distance to \((0,0)\).

retry.feedback: The centre is right. Include both coordinate changes from the centre to the origin when finding \(r^2\).

examples.title: Write the equation from a centre and one point
examples.question: Find the circle with centre \((1,3)\) passing through \((5,5)\).
solution: Every point on the circle has that squared distance, so the equation is \((x-1)^2+(y-3)^2=20\).
At \((5,5)\) the left side is \(20\), as required.

examples.title: Compare three points with the same radius
examples.question: Classify \(P(3,4)\), \(Q(-3,5)\) and \(R(1,-2)\) for \((x-1)^2+(y-3)^2=20\).
solution: For \(Q\), \(d^2=(-4)^2+2^2=20\). Hence \(Q\) is on the circle.

examples.title: Complete two squares without losing constants
examples.question: Find the centre and radius of \(x^2+y^2-2x-6y-10=0\).
solution: Add \(1\) and \(9\) to both sides. This gives \((x-1)^2+(y-3)^2=20\).
Setting each bracket to zero gives \((1,3)\). The radius is \(\sqrt{20}=2\sqrt5\).

examples.title: Find a circle from a right-angled triangle
examples.question: Find the circle through \(A(-3,1)\), \(Q(-3,5)\) and \(B(5,5)\).
solution: \(QA\) and \(QB\) are perpendicular, so the hypotenuse \(AB\) is the diameter.
The midpoint of \(AB\) is \((1,3)\), and \(AB^2=80\), so \(r^2=20\).
The circle is \((x-1)^2+(y-3)^2=20\). Substituting \(Q\) gives \(16+4=20\).

examples.title: Use the radius gradient and the point of contact
examples.question: Find the tangent and normal at \(B(5,5)\) to \((x-1)^2+(y-3)^2=20\).
solution: The point is on the circle since \(4^2+2^2=20\). The radius gradient is \(2/4=\tfrac12\).
The tangent gradient is \(-2\). Through \(B\), \(y-5=-2(x-5)\), so \(y=-2x+15\).
The normal uses the radius gradient. Its equation is \(y-5=\tfrac12(x-5)\), or \(2y=x+5\).

examples.title: Use two equal-distance conditions
examples.question: Find the circle through \((0,0)\), \((4,0)\) and \((1,3)\).
solution: The perpendicular bisector of the first two points is \(x=2\), so write the centre as \((2,k)\).
Equate the distances squared to \((0,0)\) and \((1,3)\). This gives \(4+k^2=1+(k-3)^2\), so \(6k=6\) and \(k=1\).
The radius squared is \(2^2+1^2=5\). The equation is \((x-2)^2+(y-1)^2=5\).

glossary.definition: The points at exactly distance \(r\) from the centre.
A circle containing all three vertices of a triangle.
A line touching a circle at one point, perpendicular to the radius there.
The line through the centre and the point of contact.

revision.body:
Read the centre and radius

In \((x-h)^2+(y-k)^2=r^2\), the centre is \((h,k)\) and the radius is \(r\). Compare a point's squared distance from the centre with \(r^2\) to classify it.

For expanded form, complete the \(x\)-square and the \(y\)-square separately and balance the constants. A positive result on the right gives \(r^2\).

Use the geometry before the algebra

GivenMethod
DiameterMidpoint for the centre, half the length for \(r\)
Right-angled triangleHypotenuse is the diameter
Three non-collinear pointsIntersect two perpendicular bisectors
Tangent at \(P\)Perpendicular to the radius through \(P\)
revision.checks:
• Set the brackets to zero to check the signs of the centre.
  • Take the square root of \(r^2\) for the radius.
  • Check the contact point lies on the circle.
revision.examTip: Use the point of contact in the tangent equation. A horizontal radius gives a vertical tangent, and a vertical radius gives a horizontal tangent.

orig_coordinate_geometry_line_circle.description: Study line and circle intersections for Cambridge 9709 Pure 1. Use substitutions, discriminant inequalities, chord symmetry and common points of two circles.

sections.title: How does a quadratic give both intersection points?
sections.label: Match both points
sections.intro: At an intersection with \(y=x\), both coordinates are the same. Substitute \(y=x\) into the circle to find which inputs give points on both graphs.

blocks.html: Replace one variable using the line equation. Solve the resulting quadratic and use the line to find the second coordinate for each root. Give every matched pair.
Two roots require two coordinate pairs. Checking each pair in the line prevents swapping the two \(y\)-coordinates.

blocks.prompt: Find the intersections of \(y=x+1\) and \(x^2+y^2=25\).
blocks.hint: Substitute to get \(x^2+(x+1)^2=25\). For each root, add \(1\) to get its matching \(y\).
blocks.solution: The equation reduces to \(x^2+x-12=0\), giving \(x=-4\) and \(x=3\). The pairs are \((-4,-3)\) and \((3,4)\).

retry.feedback: This is one intersection. Use the other root \(x=-4\) and pair it with \(y=x+1\).
This is one intersection. Find the other root of \(x^2+x-12=0\) too.
The roots are right. Compute \(y=x+1\) separately for each one to match the pairs.

sections.title: What changes for a vertical or horizontal line?
sections.label: Use a fixed coordinate
sections.intro: A vertical line already fixes \(x\). A horizontal line already fixes \(y\). Substitute that fixed coordinate directly.

blocks.html: Reduce to one square. For \((y-k)^2=d\), \(d>0\) gives \(k\pm\sqrt d\), \(d=0\) gives one value, and \(d<0\) gives no real values. Use the same rule for a square in \(x\).
A zero square gives a single coordinate. It represents a tangent contact when the other coordinate is fixed.

blocks.hint: Substitution gives \((y+1)^2=16\). Use both square roots.

retry.feedback: Use \(y+1=-4\) as well to find the lower point.
The centre has \(y=-1\). Add and subtract \(4\) from \(-1\).

blocks.prompt: Give the one point where \(x=6\) meets \((x-1)^2+(y+1)^2=25\).
blocks.hint: Substituting \(x=6\) uses the full squared radius in the \(x\)-term. Solve the remaining square.

retry.feedback: For the remaining square to vanish, \(y+1=0\).
That is the centre. The contact point is on the line \(x=6\).

sections.title: How can a discriminant tell whether a line touches?
sections.label: Count the intersections
sections.intro: Slide the line \(y=x+k\) up or down. With two crossings it is a secant. At a boundary it just touches, and beyond that boundary it misses. The circle here is \((x-1)^2+(y-2)^2=18\).

blocks.html:
Quadratic discriminantCommon points
\(\Delta>0\)Two distinct points
\(\Delta=0\)One point, a tangent
\(\Delta<0\)No real common points
Form the discriminant from the equation after substitution. Keep tangent values separate from any strict inequality for two points or for no points.

field.label: Values of k for two intersections

blocks.prompt: For \(x^2+y^2=8\) and \(y=x+k\), give all \(k\) for which the line meets the circle in two distinct points.
blocks.hint: After substitution the quadratic has discriminant \(64-4k^2\). Use a strict inequality for two distinct roots.

retry.feedback: The boundary values give one common point each. Use a strict interval for two distinct points.
Both signs of \(k\) can satisfy \(k^2<16\). Include all values between \(-4\) and \(4\), including zero.
Those lines miss the circle. Use \(64-4k^2>0\) for two crossings.

field.label: All values of k for tangency

blocks.prompt: For \(x^2+y^2=8\) and \(y=x+k\), give all values of \(k\) for which the line is tangent.
blocks.hint: Set \(64-4k^2=0\). Keep both signs of \(k\).

retry.feedback: That gives one tangent. The other solution of \(k^2=16\) is \(-4\).
That gives one tangent. Also use the positive solution \(k=4\).
Only the boundary values give tangency. Enter the two separate values \(-4\) and \(4\).

field.label: Values of k with no intersection

blocks.prompt: For \(x^2+y^2=8\) and \(y=x+k\), give all \(k\) for which there is no intersection.
blocks.hint: Use \(64-4k^2<0\). Which values have \(|k|>4\)?
blocks.solution: The line misses for \(k<-4\) or \(k>4\). These are the two open intervals outside the tangencies.

retry.feedback: At \(k=-4\) and \(k=4\) the line still shares one point. Exclude both endpoints.
Also include lines with \(k<-4\), below the opposite tangent.
Inside that interval the discriminant is positive. No intersection requires \(k^2>16\).

sections.title: How can symmetry give a chord length?
sections.label: Use half a chord
sections.intro: The perpendicular from the centre \(C(1,3)\) to the chord \(y=5\) meets its midpoint \(M(1,5)\). The radius to \(B(5,5)\) and the half chord \(MB\) form a right-angled triangle with \(CM\).

blocks.html: If \(d\) is the perpendicular distance from the centre to a chord and \(r\) is the radius, half the chord has length \(\sqrt{r^2-d^2}\). Double it for the full chord. A chord with distinct ends has \(d<r\).
Subtract squares in the right triangle. The half-chord length is the square root of \(r^2-d^2\).

blocks.prompt: Find the midpoint of the chord cut by \(y=5\) on \((x+1)^2+(y-2)^2=34\).
blocks.hint: Drop a vertical line from the centre \((-1,2)\) to the horizontal chord.
blocks.solution: The perpendicular meets the chord at \((-1,5)\). This is its midpoint.

retry.feedback: That is the centre. Keep its \(x\)-coordinate and use \(y=5\) to reach the chord.

blocks.prompt: Find the full length of the chord cut by \(y=5\) on \((x+1)^2+(y-2)^2=34\).
blocks.hint: The line is \(3\) units from the centre. Use \(r^2=34\) to find the half chord.
blocks.solution: The half chord has length \(\sqrt{34-9}=5\). The full chord has length \(10\).

retry.feedback: \(5\) is the distance from the chord midpoint to one endpoint. Double it.
You found the square of the half chord. Take the square root and double it.

sections.title: How can two circles give one line?
sections.label: Find a common chord
sections.intro: Both common points lie on both circles. Subtract the equations to cancel \(x^2\) and \(y^2\). For circles with different centres, this gives a straight line through any common points.

blocks.html: Write both equations with coefficients \(1\) for the squared terms. Subtract, then substitute the resulting line into either circle. Check the solutions in both original equations.
Use the line to narrow the search, then solve with a circle equation. For circles with the same centre, compare their radii directly.

blocks.prompt: Find the line through the common points of \(x^2+y^2=13\) and \((x-4)^2+y^2=5\).
blocks.hint: Subtract the first equation from the second. The change on the right is \(5-13=-8\).

retry.feedback: This would be the midpoint between the centres. The right sides differ here, so include \(5-13\) when subtracting.
The \(y^2\) terms cancel. The remaining linear equation fixes \(x=3\).

blocks.prompt: Give both common points of \(x^2+y^2=13\) and \((x-4)^2+y^2=5\).
blocks.hint: Use \(x=3\) in the first circle and take both square roots for \(y\).

retry.feedback: This is the upper point. The other root of \(y^2=4\) gives the lower point.
This is the lower point. Also take the positive root of \(y^2=4\).

examples.title: Substitute, solve, then pair the coordinates
examples.question: Find where \(y=x\) meets \((x-1)^2+(y-3)^2=20\).
solution: Substitute \(y=x\) to obtain \((x-1)^2+(x-3)^2=20\).
Expand and simplify to \(x^2-4x-5=0\). Factor as \((x+1)(x-5)=0\).
With \(y=x\), the roots \(-1\) and \(5\) give the points \((-1,-1)\) and \((5,5)\).

examples.title: Use a fixed x-coordinate
examples.question: Find where \(x=-1\) meets \((x-1)^2+(y-3)^2=20\).
solution: Substituting gives \(4+(y-3)^2=20\). Hence \((y-3)^2=16\).
Taking both square roots gives \(y-3=4\) or \(y-3=-4\), so \(y=7\) or \(y=-1\).
Use the fixed \(x=-1\) in both pairs. The points are \((-1,7)\) and \((-1,-1)\).

examples.title: Find the full range of secants and both tangents
examples.question: Classify the intersections of \(y=x+k\) with \((x-1)^2+(y-2)^2=18\) for all real \(k\).
solution: The quadratic in \(u\) has coefficients \(2,\ 2(k-1),\ (k-1)^2-18\). Thus \(\Delta=144-4(k-1)^2\).
For two points, \((k-1)^2<36\), giving \(-5<k<7\). A tangent has \(k=-5\) or \(k=7\). If \(k<-5\) or \(k>7\), the line misses the circle.

examples.title: Use the radius and the perpendicular distance
examples.question: Find the length of the chord cut by \(y=5\) on \((x-1)^2+(y-3)^2=20\).
solution: The centre is \((1,3)\), so its perpendicular distance to \(y=5\) is \(d=2\).
Half the chord is \(\sqrt{20-2^2}=\sqrt{16}=4\).
The full length is \(8\). The endpoints sit \(4\) units either side of \(M(1,5)\), at \((-3,5)\) and \((5,5)\).

examples.title: Find both ends of the common chord
examples.question: Find the common points of \(x^2+y^2=25\) and \((x-6)^2+y^2=25\).
solution: Subtracting the first equation from the second gives \(-12x+36=0\). Hence every common point has \(x=3\).
Substituting into \(x^2+y^2=25\) gives \(y^2=16\). Use both roots.
The two points are \((3,4)\) and \((3,-4)\). Both satisfy the second equation too.

glossary.definition: A line meeting a circle at two distinct points.
A line meeting a circle at one point.
The segment joining two points on a circle.
The expression \(b^2-4ac\) which determines the number of distinct real roots of a quadratic.

revision.body:
Substitute before counting or solving

Insert the line into the circle. Solve the quadratic and find the second coordinate for each root. Substitute \(x=c\) directly for a vertical line.

DiscriminantIntersection
\(\Delta>0\)Two distinct points
\(\Delta=0\)One tangent point
\(\Delta<0\)No intersection

Use chord geometry

The perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord. If its distance is \(d<r\), the chord length is \(2\sqrt{r^2-d^2}\). For two circles with different centres, subtract their expanded equations and substitute the resulting line back into a circle.
revision.checks:
• Pair each root with its own second coordinate.
  • Keep tangent boundaries out of strict secant ranges.
  • Double a half chord to get its full length.
revision.examTip: Give all parameter intervals and all boundary values requested. Check any stated intersection in both equations.
